heading: Background
html:
An acute red, hot, swollen joint should be treated as septic arthritis until proven otherwise. Delayed treatment risks rapid joint destruction and significant mortality. The commonest alternative diagnoses are crystal arthropathy (gout / pseudogout) and a flare of osteoarthritis.

Prosthetic joints are different. Any suspicion of infection in a prosthetic joint is managed by orthopaedics from the outset — diagnosis and treatment decisions (including aspiration and antibiotics) are made in secondary care.

heading: Assessment
html:
Two questions determine the pathway:

1. Is there a prosthetic joint in situ, or a penetrating wound overlying the joint? If yes → same-day orthopaedic discussion (see Who to Refer). Do not investigate further in the community.

2. In a native joint without a penetrating wound, are any red flags present?

Red flags — same-day orthopaedic discussion

  • Extreme pain on joint movement
  • Systemically unwell (with or without temperature)
  • Pyrexia
  • Unable to weight bear

Features supporting primary care management with early review

  • Good range of joint movement
  • Able to weight bear
  • No pyrexia
  • History of gout or osteoarthritis

heading: Primary care management
html:
Only for the patient with no red flags: good range of movement, weight bearing, apyrexial, with a history of gout or osteoarthritis.

  • Bloods: FBC, CRP, ESR
  • Analgesia — consider NSAIDs if no contraindication
  • Review in 24 hours

At the 24-hour review:

Worsening

  • Discuss with orthopaedics if the picture is infective
  • Discuss with rheumatology if the picture is inflammatory

Improving

  • Continue management and review at 4–6 weeks

If at any point red flags develop, move to same-day orthopaedic discussion.

heading: Who to refer
html:
Same-day discussion with orthopaedics on call

  • Prosthetic joint in situ with a red, hot, swollen joint
  • Penetrating wound overlying the joint (wound washout is best performed in theatre)
  • Native joint with any red flag: extreme pain on movement, systemic upset (with or without temperature), pyrexia, unable to weight bear

Do not aspirate a prosthetic joint. Do not start antibiotics where there is a prosthetic joint — both compromise the definitive diagnosis and management in theatre.

After 24-hour review — if worsening

  • Discuss with orthopaedics if infective features predominate
  • Discuss with rheumatology if inflammatory features predominate

heading: Who not to refer
html:
Patients suitable for primary care management with early review rather than referral:

  • Native joint, no penetrating wound, and no red flags — good range of movement, able to weight bear, apyrexial — particularly with a history of gout or osteoarthritis. Manage with bloods, analgesia and 24-hour review.
  • Patients improving at the 24-hour review — continue primary care management and review at 4–6 weeks.

Keep the threshold for discussion low: if the presentation is not following the expected course of a crystal or osteoarthritis flare, discuss the same day.
